name: UNIKOTECH and early DPRK software-export marketing (2000–2004 historical context)

attribution.legal_posture: Historical scholarly and policy sources describe disclosed commercial or cooperative software activity; allegation, adjudication, sanctions designation, modern fraudulent-employment finding, and current-control claim require separate evidence.

caveats: Historical paid software work, training, joint development, product marketing, and overseas technical labor remain distinct from false-identity remote employment, laptop farming, unauthorized employer access, malicious cyber activity, or sanctions evasion unless an explicit source bridge connects them.

Marketing or selling DPRK-developed software abroad supplies commercial context; modern fraudulent employment, malicious code, sanctions evasion, and knowing facilitation require separate evidence. Person-level attribution and current-control claims require separate evidence from this record.
These closed historical relationships provide historical context; worker, employee, persona, account, current company, and present operation require current source evidence.

Retain for historical export-channel context. Before normalization, confirm whether contemporary corporate records or later official sources clarify the unnamed DPRK software organization and whether the entity continued after the cited period.
The named South Korean or foreign organizations are described in source reporting; knowing-facilitator status requires separate evidence.

infrastructure.statement: Marketing or selling DPRK-developed software abroad is not by itself evidence of modern fraudulent employment, malicious code, sanctions evasion, or knowing facilitation. No person-level attribution or current-control claim should be derived from this record.

sources.support: Separates true joint software development from South Korean marketing and representation of DPRK software in an external market, supporting a distinct historical export/representation category. Source scope: The chapter separates joint software development and marketing from other IT cooperation, names Samsung Electronics, Hanabiz.com, Entrac, Chosun Computer Center, and Dandong training centers, and frames the model as low-capital, labor-intensive commercial cooperation rather than concealed remote hiring. Evidence boundary: Government-hosted scholarly analysis. Several details reproduce then-current company or press reporting and should remain attributed to the chapter rather than presented as independently adjudicated facts. PDF creation date; the reviewed chapter itself identifies the 2005 edited volume but does not print a separate day-level publication date

Reports that IMRI jointly established UNIKOTECH with a DPRK software-development organization and a Tokyo company in July 2000, with communications solutions and Japanese sales as its stated focus. Source scope: The article describes disclosed commercial cooperation: a Samsung–Chosun Computer Center software center in Beijing, UNIKOTECH as a sales-oriented joint venture, and the Hana Program Center in Dandong filling software-development orders from South Korea and China using DPRK labor. Evidence boundary: Reputable academic source based partly on cited contemporary reporting and disclosed author interviews. It is historical secondary evidence, not a current corporate-registry record or proof of later illicit conduct. issue-level month inferred from the journal issue label Fall 2004; no day is printed in the reviewed PDF
